explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The Gazites surrounded the place and lay in wait for Samson at the city gate. They stayed quiet all night, saying, “Let us wait until dawn; then we will kill him.” That's a heavy plan, and the text doesn't soften it. Hold on to it, because it makes what Samson does at midnight hit even harder.

Not quite, baker, and it's a heavy one. The Gazites surrounded the place where Samson was and lay in wait at the city gate. They were quiet all night, saying, “Let us wait until dawn; then we will kill him.” So the plan was real, and it was set for dawn.

Yes, friend! Samson got up at midnight, took hold of the doors of the city gate and both gateposts, and pulled them out, bar and all. No lock, no latch, no problem. The Gazites were waiting quietly at that very gate, and I'd love to have seen their faces in the morning.

Ha! Picture Samson tapping politely and saying, "Anybody got the key?" That's not what happened. The text says he took hold of the doors of the city gate and both gateposts and pulled them out, bar and all. When a gate's in Samson's way, the gate loses.

Good guess, baker, but he never bothered with the wall. The text says he took hold of the doors of the city gate and both gateposts and pulled them out, bar and all. He went right through the gate, and he took the gate with him. Climbing is for folks who can't carry a whole entrance.

explanations.answer: Where his great strength comes from
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The lords of the Philistines told Delilah, the woman Samson loved, to "…find out the source of his great strength and how we can overpower him…" They weren't asking about his schedule or his hiding spots. They wanted the secret behind that strength, and they planned to use it against him.

Close, but that's not what they asked, friend. The lords of the Philistines told Delilah, the woman Samson loved in the Valley of Sorek, to "…find out the source of his great strength and how we can overpower him…" They wanted the secret behind his strength.

explanations.answer: When he plans to attack next
explanations.explanation: Nope, baker, but I see the thinking. The lords of the Philistines asked Delilah, the woman Samson loved, to "…find out the source of his great strength and how we can overpower him…" Nothing about his battle plans. They were after the secret of his strength, and how to tie him up and subdue him.

You got it, baker. Each lord promised Delilah eleven hundred shekels of silver. That's from every single lord, not one pooled-up pot. The text names the silver and nothing else, so that's the whole offer.

explanations.answer: A house in the Valley of Sorek
explanations.explanation: A house would be a nice reward, but the text doesn't offer one. The lords said, "Then each one of us will give you eleven hundred shekels of silver." It was silver, and it was from each lord.

That would've been a big promotion, friend, but the text never offers it. The lords said, "Then each one of us will give you eleven hundred shekels of silver." The offer was silver and only silver. And it was a full amount from every lord, not a share.

Right, baker. Samson said that with seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, he would "…become as weak as any other man." That's what he told Delilah. We'll see in a moment whether it was true.

Gentle would be a surprise for the man who just carried off a city gate, baker! But that's not the word. Samson said he'd "…become as weak as any other man." He was talking about his strength, not his manners.

Slow is a fair guess, friend, but Samson didn't say it. He told Delilah that with seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, he would "…become as weak as any other man." The word is weak. It's all about his strength.
That's it, baker! Samson snapped the bowstrings "…like a strand of yarn seared by a flame." The men were hidden in the room, and nothing came of it. Delilah's first try was a flop.

They didn't hold, baker. The text says he snapped the bowstrings "…like a strand of yarn seared by a flame." Seven of them, and they went like nothing. So Samson's first answer to Delilah didn't work.

explanations.answer: He gives up without a fight
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. When Delilah called out that the Philistines were there, Samson snapped the bowstrings "…like a strand of yarn seared by a flame." There was no giving up at all. The ties were the ones that gave out.

Not quite, baker. The bowstrings snapped, but the text says, "So the source of his strength remained unknown." Samson had given her a made-up answer, and it showed. So Delilah was still in the dark about his secret.
Right, baker. The text says, "So the source of his strength remained unknown." The bowstrings snapped, so they didn't subdue Samson. His answer hadn't given her the secret.

explanations.answer: He snaps them off his arms
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Delilah tied him up with new ropes and called out, and he snapped the ropes off his arms "…like they were threads." The men were hidden in her room again, and again it did nothing. That's two tries, and two tries wasted.

They didn't hold, friend. The text says he snapped the ropes off his arms "…like they were threads." Brand-new ropes, never used, and they went like thread anyway. Samson's second answer didn't help Delilah any more than the first.

explanations.answer: He slips out and runs off
explanations.explanation: There was no slipping out, baker. The text says he snapped the ropes off his arms "…like they were threads." He didn't wriggle free. He broke them.

explanations.answer: Weaving his braids into a loom
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Samson told her, "If you weave the seven braids of my head into the web of a loom and tighten it with a pin, I will become as weak as any other man." This one finally has something to do with his head. Notice how much closer it is to the truth than ropes and bowstrings.

explanations.answer: Locking him in an iron cage
explanations.explanation: A cage sounds serious, friend, but he never said it. Samson told her, "If you weave the seven braids of my head into the web of a loom and tighten it with a pin, I will become as weak as any other man." This time he brought up his hair, and his seven braids.

That's the same kind of answer as the first two, baker, but he changed it this time. Samson said, "If you weave the seven braids of my head into the web of a loom and tighten it with a pin, I will become as weak as any other man." No more bowstrings or ropes. This time it was his seven braids.

That's right, baker. Samson woke up from his sleep and pulled out the pin with the loom and the web. Delilah had called out, and he pulled it all out like it was nothing. That's three tries and three misses for her.

It's true, baker. The text says he awoke from his sleep and pulled out the pin with the loom and the web. His braids were woven in, and still he woke and pulled it all out. So Delilah's third try didn't hold him either.
That's it, baker. The text says she "…pressed him daily with her words and pleaded until he was sick to death…" Daily means every day, with no days off. I think that'd wear down anybody's patience.
Once a month would've been a breeze, friend! But the text says she "…pressed him daily with her words…" Daily means every day. She pleaded until he was "…sick to death…"

That would've given Samson six quiet days a week, baker. But the text says she "…pressed him daily with her words and pleaded until he was sick to death…" Daily means every day. It doesn't pick out one special day.

explanations.answer: His hair has never been cut
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Samson said, "My hair has never been cut, because I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb." That's the real secret, at last. It's a heavy moment, because he finally told her all that was in his heart.

No ring in this story, baker. Samson told Delilah, "My hair has never been cut, because I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb." The secret was about his hair. His mother comes up only in how long he's been a Nazirite, from her womb.

That's not what he said, friend. Samson told Delilah, "My hair has never been cut, because I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb." He didn't mention praying at all. He pointed to his hair.
Right, baker. Samson said, "If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I will become as weak as any other man." That was the part Delilah had been after all along. Now she had the real answer.
Courage isn't the word, baker. Samson said, "If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I will become as weak as any other man." It's his strength, the thing Delilah kept asking about.

Wisdom is a good thing to lose sleep over, friend, but that's not the word. Samson said, "If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I will become as weak as any other man." He was talking about his strength, the very thing she'd been asking about.

Not this time, baker. The text says, "When Delilah realized that he had revealed to her all that was in his heart…" she sent a message to the lords of the Philistines. She knew he'd told her everything, so she didn't hold back. The earlier times, she called out to Samson that the Philistines were there.

That's right, baker. The text says Delilah realized he had revealed to her all that was in his heart, and she sent this message to the lords: “Come up once more…” She wasn't unsure at all. This time she knew.
Yes, baker. The text says the lords of the Philistines came to her, "…bringing the money in their hands." That's the silver they had promised. They showed up with it ready.

Swords are a reasonable guess, friend, but the text doesn't say so. It says the lords of the Philistines came to her, "…bringing the money in their hands." The thing in their hands was the money they'd promised Delilah.
Gifts for Samson aren't in the text, baker. It says the lords of the Philistines came to Delilah "…bringing the money in their hands." It was the money, the silver they'd promised her.

explanations.answer: The LORD had departed from him
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker, and it's a heavy line. Samson thought, “I will escape as I did before and shake myself free.” But the text says, "…he did not know that the LORD had departed from him." He was counting on the old way, and the old strength was gone.

explanations.answer: The lords had brought more men
explanations.explanation: That's a good guess, baker, but it's not what Samson missed. Samson thought, “I will escape as I did before and shake myself free.” The text says, "…he did not know that the LORD had departed from him." That's the thing he didn't know.

Nothing about locked doors, friend. Samson thought, “I will escape as I did before and shake myself free.” The text says, "…he did not know that the LORD had departed from him." That was the thing he didn't know.

That's right, baker, and it's a sad scene. The Philistines brought Samson down to Gaza, where he was bound with bronze shackles and forced to grind grain in the prison. He was the same man who carried off that city's gate. I think this one hurts to read.

Not the temple, baker, and this part is heavy. The text says Samson was bound with bronze shackles in Gaza and forced to grind grain in the prison. He'd been brought down to the very city where he once pulled out the gate. I think it's hard to see him there.

It was no palace, friend, and this part is heavy. The text says Samson was brought down to Gaza, bound with bronze shackles and forced to grind grain in the prison. He was a prisoner there, with no comfort in it.

Yes, baker. The text says, "…the hair of his head began to grow back after it had been shaved." That's a small line, but it's there after a very dark scene. I'll leave it right there and let you wonder about it.

It's true, baker. The text says, "…the hair of his head began to grow back after it had been shaved." It's a small line after a very dark scene. I'll leave it right there, because the story isn't done.
